description: Neutralisation, pH, and the salts we make from acids in the lab.
content_html:
Acids, Bases and the pH Scale

An acid is a substance that releases hydrogen ions (\ (H^+\)) in water. A base is a substance that neutralises an acid. An alkali is a soluble base — it produces hydroxide ions (\ (OH^-\)) in solution. All alkalis are bases, but not all bases are alkalis (some bases are insoluble, such as copper oxide).

The pH scale runs from 0 to 14. A pH of 7 is neutral; below 7 is acidic; above 7 is alkaline. pH is measured using universal indicator (colour matched to a chart) or a digital pH probe (more precise). The scale is logarithmic — each unit change represents a tenfold change in hydrogen ion concentration.

Key Fact

Acids produce \(H^+\) ions in water; alkalis produce \(OH^-\) ions. Neutralisation: \(H^+ + OH^- \rightarrow H_2O\). pH 0–6 = acidic; 7 = neutral; 8–14 = alkaline.

Neutralisation Reactions

Neutralisation is the reaction between an acid and a base. The general ionic equation is:

$$H^+ + OH^- \rightarrow H_2O$$

The products are a salt and water. The key reactions of acids that produce salts are:

  • Acid + metal → salt + hydrogen. E.g. \(Mg + 2HCl \rightarrow MgCl_2 + H_2\)
  • Acid + metal oxide → salt + water. E.g. \(CuO + H_2SO_4 \rightarrow CuSO_4 + H_2O\)
  • Acid + metal hydroxide → salt + water. E.g. \(NaOH + HCl \rightarrow NaCl + H_2O\)
  • Acid + metal carbonate → salt + water + carbon dioxide. E.g. \(CaCO_3 + 2HCl \rightarrow CaCl_2 + H_2O + CO_2\)

Naming Salts and Making Them

A salt takes its name from the metal and the acid. Hydrochloric acid (\ (HCl\)) produces chlorides; sulfuric acid (\ (H_2SO_4\)) produces sulfates; nitric acid (\ (HNO_3\)) produces nitrates. To predict a salt, name the metal first, then the acid type — e.g. zinc + hydrochloric acid gives zinc chloride.

To prepare a pure, dry salt: add an excess of insoluble base (e.g. copper oxide) to a warm acid (e.g. sulfuric acid) and stir. The excess solid ensures all acid is used up. Filter off the unreacted solid. Gently heat the filtrate to evaporate some water, then leave to cool so crystals form. Filter the crystals and dry at low temperature. The excess base guarantees no acid remains in the product — this is the key step that distinguishes this method from a titration.

Key Fact

HCl → chlorides. \(H_2SO_4\) → sulfates. \(HNO_3\) → nitrates. Predict any salt: metal name + acid type. Example: magnesium + nitric acid = magnesium nitrate.

Titration

Titration is used to find the exact volume of acid needed to neutralise a known volume of alkali (or vice versa). The method uses a burette to deliver acid accurately, a pipette to measure a fixed volume of alkali into a conical flask, and an indicator to detect the end point (when the solution changes colour, showing neutralisation is complete).

Set up a burette filled with acid and record the initial reading. Using a pipette and filler, transfer a fixed volume of alkali into a conical flask. Add two or three drops of indicator (e.g. phenolphthalein or methyl orange). Slowly add acid from the burette, swirling the flask. Add dropwise near the end point — the indicator will change colour permanently when neutralisation is complete. Record the final burette reading. The titre is the volume of acid added (final reading minus initial reading). Repeat until two concordant results are obtained (within 0.10 cm³ of each other). Average the concordant titres for accuracy.

Strong acids (hydrochloric, sulfuric, nitric) fully ionise in water — every molecule releases its \(H^+\) ions. Weak acids (ethanoic, citric) only partially ionise, establishing an equilibrium. At the same concentration, a strong acid has a lower pH than a weak acid because it produces more \(H^+\) ions. Concentration and strength are different properties — a dilute strong acid can have the same pH as a concentrated weak acid.

Indicators and Measuring pH

An indicator is a substance whose colour depends on pH. Universal indicator is a mixture of dyes that shows a range of colours: red and orange for strongly acidic solutions, green for neutral, blue and violet for alkaline solutions. However, it gives only an approximate pH reading. For more accurate measurement, a pH probe is used — these give a numerical reading to several decimal places and are essential in research and industry.

Phenolphthalein is a specific indicator that is colourless in acid and turns pink in alkali. Methyl orange is yellow in alkali and red in acid. The choice of indicator in a titration depends on the strength of the acid and alkali being used. For a strong acid reacting with a strong alkali, either indicator works well. The end point shows a permanent colour change that means exactly enough acid has been added to neutralise all the alkali.

Everyday Examples of Neutralisation

Neutralisation reactions are not just laboratory techniques — they are at work in agriculture, medicine, and industry. Farmers add powdered limestone (calcium carbonate) or quicklime (calcium oxide) to acidic soils to raise the pH, making conditions better for crops. Indigestion remedies work by neutralising excess stomach acid (hydrochloric acid) with a mild alkali such as magnesium hydroxide or calcium carbonate. Toothpastes often contain mild alkalis to neutralise the acids produced by bacteria in the mouth, which cause tooth decay. Understanding which acid is present and which base will neutralise it efficiently is a practical application of this chemistry.
exam_tip_html: In questions about making salts, a common error is not explaining why an excess of solid is added — always state it ensures all acid is neutralised. For titration questions, name the dependent variable (volume of acid added), the independent variable (concentration of alkali or acid being found), and the controlled variables (volume of alkali, indicator used, temperature). When asked about strong vs weak acids, do not confuse strength with concentration: a strong acid fully ionises; concentration refers to the amount of acid dissolved per litre.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Acids produce \(H^+\) ions; alkalis produce \(OH^-\) ions. Neutralisation (\(H^+ + OH^- \rightarrow H_2O\)) produces a salt and water; the salt is named from the metal and the acid type (chloride, sulfate, or nitrate).
  • A soluble salt is made by adding an excess of insoluble base to acid, filtering off the excess solid, then crystallising and drying the product; titration is used to find the precise volumes needed for neutralisation without excess.
  • Neutralisation has everyday applications: liming acidic soils, indigestion remedies, and toothpaste all rely on the reaction between an acid and a base to adjust pH.

practice_questions.text: Write the ionic equation for neutralisation.
practice_questions.marks: H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O (1 mark). State symbols not required unless the question asks for them.

practice_questions.text: Name the salt produced when zinc reacts with sulfuric acid.
practice_questions.marks: Zinc sulfate (1 mark). No mark for zinc sulfide (wrong anion) or zinc chloride (wrong acid).

practice_questions.text: A student adds hydrochloric acid to sodium hydroxide solution. Describe how they would use an indicator to determine when neutralisation is complete.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: add a few drops of a suitable indicator (e.g. phenolphthalein or methyl orange) to the alkali (1); add acid from the burette slowly, swirling the flask (1); the end point is when the indicator changes colour permanently and does not return to the original colour (1). Secure: three steps. Developing: indicator named and colour change described, method incomplete. Emerging: one step.

practice_questions.text: Outline a method to make a pure, dry sample of magnesium chloride from magnesium oxide and hydrochloric acid.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: add excess magnesium oxide to warm hydrochloric acid and stir (1); filter to remove excess magnesium oxide (1); heat the filtrate to evaporate water until crystals begin to form, then leave to cool (1); filter the crystals and dry them at low temperature (1). Secure: all four stages. Developing: three stages. Emerging: two stages.

practice_questions.text: A student carries out a titration using sodium hydroxide solution and hydrochloric acid. Their results give three titres: 24.30 cm³, 24.25 cm³, 24.80 cm³. Calculate the mean titre the student should use.
practice_questions.marks: Identifies that 24.80 cm³ is anomalous/not concordant with the others and excludes it (1); mean = (24.30 + 24.25) ÷ 2 = 24.28 cm³ (1). Mastering: anomaly identified and mean correct. Secure: correct answer. Developing: calculates mean of all three without excluding anomaly. Emerging: no anomaly identified.

practice_questions.text: Hydrochloric acid and ethanoic acid are both acids, but at the same concentration hydrochloric acid has a lower pH. Explain why, and what this tells us about their degree of ionisation in water.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: hydrochloric acid is a strong acid and fully ionises in water, producing the maximum number of H⁺ ions (1); ethanoic acid is a weak acid that only partially ionises — an equilibrium is established (1); more H⁺ ions in the hydrochloric acid solution gives a lower pH at the same concentration (1). Secure: three points. Developing: two points. Emerging: one point.

knowledge_checks.q: What ions does an alkali produce when dissolved in water?
Which acid produces sulfate salts when it reacts with metals or bases?
The pH scale runs from 0 to 14. A solution with pH 7 is _____.
When copper oxide reacts with sulfuric acid, the salt produced is copper _____.
Match each acid to the type of salt it forms.

flashcard_questions.q: What type of ion does an acid release in water?
What type of ion does an alkali release in water?
Write the ionic equation for neutralisation.
What salt does hydrochloric acid produce?
What salt does sulfuric acid produce?
What salt does nitric acid produce?
Why is excess insoluble base added when making a soluble salt from acid?
flashcard_questions.a: To ensure all the acid is neutralised, leaving no acid in the final product.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the purpose of a titration in chemistry?
flashcard_questions.a: To find the exact volume of one solution needed to neutralise another.
An acid that fully ionises in water, releasing the maximum number of H⁺ ions.

flashcard_questions.q: How does a weak acid differ from a strong acid at the same concentration?
flashcard_questions.a: A weak acid partially ionises, producing fewer H⁺ ions and so having a higher pH.

flashcard_questions.q: Name the salt produced when magnesium reacts with hydrochloric acid.

glossary_terms.definition: A substance that produces hydrogen ions (H⁺) when dissolved in water; acids have a pH below 7.
A substance that can neutralise an acid; alkalis are soluble bases.
A soluble base that produces hydroxide ions (OH⁻) when dissolved in water; alkalis have a pH above 7.
A scale from 0 to 14 measuring how acidic or alkaline a solution is; pH below 7 is acidic, 7 is neutral, above 7 is alkaline.
A reaction between an acid and a base that produces a salt and water, with the ionic equation H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O.
A compound formed when the hydrogen in an acid is replaced by a metal ion; named from the metal and the acid type.
A technique used to find the volume of one solution needed to exactly neutralise another, using an indicator to identify the end point.
An acid that fully ionises in water, releasing the maximum number of H⁺ ions; examples include hydrochloric, sulfuric, and nitric acid.
An acid that only partially ionises in water, establishing an equilibrium; examples include ethanoic acid and citric acid.
A substance that changes colour reversibly when pH changes, used to show whether a solution is acidic, neutral or alkaline.
An electronic instrument that measures pH accurately by detecting hydrogen ion concentration in a solution.
